ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in the invoice list ORDER BY clause
ruled_out.killed_by: Invoice::sortColumn (app/Models/Invoice.php:56) is a strict in_array($requested, SORTABLE, true) allowlist that falls back to SORTABLE[0]; $dir on line 27 is a two-way ternary yielding only 'asc' or 'desc'.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the aging window parameter
ruled_out.killed_by: $days is cast with (int) at line 71 before it reaches the interval literal, so only digits can arrive.

ruled_out.assertion: Command injection in the PDF renderer's exec() call
ruled_out.killed_by: $template is checked against the TEMPLATES allowlist at line 27 and throws otherwise; $layout and $source are escapeshellarg'd; the unescaped $target is built by sprintf('%s/invoice-%d.pdf', ...) from a constructor default and an integer-cast id.

ruled_out.assertion: Forgeable payment webhook signature
ruled_out.killed_by: The middleware computes hash_hmac('sha256', t.'.'.rawBody, secret) and compares with hash_equals (line 45), rejects a timestamp outside 300s (line 33) and refuses to run when the secret is unset (line 39). All three controls are on the path.

ruled_out.assertion: Password reset token generated from md5(email . microtime . mt_rand)
ruled_out.killed_by: legacyResetToken is protected and has no caller: a grep for the symbol across the whole tree returns only the declaration at AuthController.php:103. The live flow at line 65 uses bin2hex(random_bytes(32)) stored as a sha256 hash.

ruled_out.assertion: Log injection through the email logged on a failed login
ruled_out.killed_by: The value logged is $credentials['email'], the output of $request->validate(['email' => ['required','email']]) at line 24, so it cannot carry CR or LF.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through window_hours in the evaluation series
ruled_out.killed_by: window_hours is extracted as a typed i64 by Path<(String, i64)> (routes.rs:87) and clamped with .clamp(1, 720) at routes.rs:96 before reaching the format!.

ruled_out.assertion: Cross-tenant flag disclosure via load_flag(id) with no tenant predicate
ruled_out.killed_by: Both callers resolve the id through flag_id_for_key (store.rs:37), which binds tenant_id as $1: routes.rs:71 for detail and routes.rs:91 for series.

ruled_out.assertion: MD5 used for webhook signing
ruled_out.killed_by: legacy_digest carries #[allow(dead_code)] and has no caller in the crate; notify_rollout uses sign() with HMAC-SHA256 at line 25.

ruled_out.assertion: Permissive CORS allowing any origin on the edge-flags API
ruled_out.killed_by: The AllowOrigin::any() layer is attached only to the probes router (main.rs:113-116), which serves /healthz and /buildinfo, is GET-only and does not set allow_credentials. The API router gets console_cors with a configured origin list (main.rs:101-111, 119).

ruled_out.assertion: MD5 API-key digest with a non-constant-time comparison
ruled_out.killed_by: The scheme is never registered: Program.cs:21-25 adds only JwtBearer, and a grep for AddScheme across fleet-api returns nothing. The LegacyKeys configuration section it reads does not exist in either appsettings file either.

ruled_out.assertion: JWT signing key committed in appsettings.json
ruled_out.killed_by: The code reads config["Jwt:SigningKey"] (TokenService.cs:20 and 41), not Jwt:FixtureSigningKey, and the committed value is the published worked example from RFC 7515 appendix A.1 - public by construction, so it is not a secret.

ruled_out.assertion: Wildcard CORS origin in the production settings
ruled_out.killed_by: Cors:AllowedOrigins has zero readers in the tree; Program.cs:49 builds the console policy from Cors:PublicOrigins, which in this file is the single origin https://console.fleetline.example.

ruled_out.assertion: Mass assignment of IsFactoryUnlocked on device registration
ruled_out.killed_by: The binding target is the DeviceRegistration record declared at line 117 with exactly two members, Serial and Model; the entity is constructed field by field on lines 79-85 and IsFactoryUnlocked is never assigned from the body.

ruled_out.assertion: Path traversal in the firmware bundle path
ruled_out.killed_by: channel is bound as the FirmwareChannel enum (Models/FleetModels.cs:9-15); ASP.NET Core model binding rejects any segment outside the four members before the action runs, so Path.Combine only ever receives one of four literals.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the queue parameter in queue_board
ruled_out.killed_by: queue_id is produced by int(request.GET.get("queue", 0)) at line 74, so only an integer can reach the f-string; the organization filter beside it is bound as %s.

ruled_out.assertion: Command injection in the attachment virus scan
ruled_out.killed_by: stored_path (tickets/models.py:84) is os.path.join(ATTACHMENT_ROOT, uuid4().hex + extension), and extension is set only from the ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS allowlist check at tickets/forms.py:28; the browser-supplied name is stored in display_name and never used as a path.

ruled_out.assertion: ticket_export is reachable without authentication because it lacks @login_required
ruled_out.killed_by: LoginRequiredMiddleware (tickets/middleware.py:17, registered at config/settings.py:51) redirects any anonymous request whose path is not in PUBLIC_PATHS, and PUBLIC_PATHS (settings.py:56-61) does not contain /tickets/export/.

ruled_out.assertion: Reflected XSS in the JSON form-error responses
ruled_out.killed_by: json.dumps(form.errors) serialises Django's own validation messages; neither CommentForm nor AttachmentForm (tickets/forms.py) produces a message that echoes submitted content, so no attacker-controlled string reaches the response body.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in the account_balance_at dynamic statement
ruled_out.killed_by: p_account_id is declared bigint, so only digits can be concatenated, and p_asof is passed with USING at line 19. The function is SECURITY INVOKER, so the entries RLS policy (002_rls.sql:65-67) still constrains the rows.

ruled_out.assertion: Live pgbouncer SCRAM verifiers committed to the repository
ruled_out.killed_by: The file documents its own status on lines 1-7 and the claim checks out against the script: provision.sh:101-106 writes /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt from the secret store on every run and never copies this sample. The values are also structurally filler, not derived verifiers.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the LIMIT clause in listNotes
ruled_out.killed_by: The only caller is recentNotes (app/actions/notes.ts:35), which passes the output of ListInput.parse - z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(200) at line 18 - so limit can only be an integer in 1..200.

ruled_out.assertion: Stored XSS via dangerouslySetInnerHTML on the note body
ruled_out.killed_by: note.html is only ever produced by renderNoteHtml (lib/policy.ts:66), configured with html:false (line 35) and a link_open rule that rewrites any href outside http/https/mailto to '#' (lines 47-59). Both write paths go through it: app/actions/notes.ts:49 and :75.

ruled_out.assertion: MD5 with a non-constant-time comparison in legacy session verification
ruled_out.killed_by: verifyLegacySession has no caller: a grep across notes-workspace returns only its declaration at lib/session.ts:60. The three live consumers all call readSession.

ruled_out.assertion: Authentication bypass through unanchored public-prefix matching in the middleware
ruled_out.killed_by: The startsWith match is unanchored, but no route in the tree extends /sign-in, /sign-up, /legal or /shared, so no protected path is shadowed in what ships. The pattern is worth changing to a segment-aware comparison; it is not reachable here.

ruled_out.assertion: Log injection through the edge-flags webhook warning lines
ruled_out.killed_by: The subscriber is initialised with tracing_subscriber::fmt().json() at main.rs:76, so each event is emitted as one JSON object with control characters escaped in field values; the interpolated reqwest error cannot forge a record in that format.

findings.title: SQL injection in the invoice type-ahead search
findings.evidence: Line 47 takes $term = trim($request->query('q','')) straight from the query string and line 57 splices it into a raw DB::select as "number like '%{$term}%' or notes like '%{$term}%'". The only bound parameter in the statement is account_id. No escaping, casting or allowlist sits between the request and the string.
findings.impact: Any authenticated portal user breaks out of the LIKE literal and rewrites the WHERE clause, which also defeats the account_id predicate that is the tenant boundary: invoices, notes and any other table the DB user can reach are readable, and on a stacked-query-capable driver writable.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term as a parameter: "... number like ? or notes like ?" with ['%'.$term.'%', ...] passed in the bindings array, alongside the account_id binding already there.

triage.reason: $term originates at InvoiceController.php:47 in $request->query('q') and reaches line 57 with only trim() applied; nothing constrains its character set.

The route (routes/web.php:38) carries only the 'auth' middleware; there is no query-layer control in the tree, and the sibling statements at lines 29 and 73 show the project binds parameters when it intends to.

findings.title: Invoice detail is fetched by id with no account scoping (BOLA)
findings.evidence: show() runs Invoice::with('account')->findOrFail($id) on the bare model. The two sibling handlers in the same file that take the same {id} route parameter both scope first: update() at line 101 and download() at line 113 use Invoice::where('account_id', $request->user()->account_id)->findOrFail($id). There is no authorize() call and no policy invocation in show().
findings.impact: Any signed-in customer reads any other customer's invoice, including the joined account record, by incrementing the id in /invoices/{id}. Invoice numbers, totals, memo lines and account details of every tenant are exposed.
findings.recommendation: Scope the lookup the way the siblings do: Invoice::where('account_id', $request->user()->account_id)->with('account')->findOrFail($id), or register an InvoicePolicy and call $this->authorize('view', $invoice).

triage.reason: No unskippable layer applies the scope: if one did, the explicit where('account_id', ...) on lines 101 and 113 of this same file would be redundant. That asymmetry is the evidence.
The route sits inside the 'auth' group at routes/web.php:40; it is a per-customer resource, not a public one.
The model (app/Models/Invoice.php) carries total_cents, paid_at, credit_applied_cents and notes, and the handler eager-loads the owning Account.

findings.title: forceFill($request->all()) makes the model's fillable and guarded lists inert
findings.evidence: Line 104 is $invoice->forceFill($request->all())->save(). Invoice declares $fillable (Invoice.php:21) and $guarded = ['account_id','total_cents','paid_at','credit_applied_cents'] (Invoice.php:29). forceFill is Eloquent's explicit unguarded path: it fills inside unguarded(), so both lists are bypassed by construction. $request->all() is the raw request payload.
findings.impact: A customer editing their own invoice adds total_cents, paid_at or credit_applied_cents to the PATCH body and the values persist. An invoice can be marked paid, its balance zeroed, or its account_id rewritten to move the record to another tenant. The guard list that a reviewer reads as the control does nothing.
findings.recommendation: Replace with $invoice->fill($request->validate([...]))->save(), validating an explicit allowlist of the fields the edit form is allowed to change (number, status, due_at, notes, po_reference).

triage.reason: $guarded at Invoice.php:29 is the apparent control and forceFill() is defined to bypass it; it is additionally inert because a non-empty $fillable takes precedence over $guarded in Eloquent.
total_cents, paid_at and credit_applied_cents are the money fields of a billing record, and account_id is the tenant key.

findings.title: A working APP_KEY is committed as the default in config/app.php
findings.evidence: 'key' => env('APP_KEY', 'base64:c2FtcGxlLWtleS1mb3ItYmlsbGluZy1wb3J0YWwtMDE='). The default decodes to a 32-byte ASCII string, which is a valid AES-256-CBC key that Laravel will accept and use rather than fail on. Two lines up, 'env' => env('APP_ENV', 'production') makes production the default posture for the same file.
findings.impact: Where APP_KEY is not set in the environment, session payloads, encrypted cookies, signed URLs and anything passed through Crypt are protected by a key that is published in the repository: an attacker forges session cookies and signed links at will. Independently of deployment, the key is compromised from the moment it was versioned and needs rotation.
findings.recommendation: Remove the default so the framework fails closed when APP_KEY is absent, run php artisan key:generate per environment, and rotate the published key.

triage.reason: It is not a placeholder such as ${VAR} or changeme; it is a syntactically valid base64 key of the right length that the framework will use silently.
No .env, deployment manifest or CI configuration is present in the tree, so whether the shipped environment sets APP_KEY cannot be established here. Per the cap this finding is reported as probable.

findings.title: Debug mode defaults to on and the file documents that it stays on
findings.evidence: 'debug' => (bool) env('APP_DEBUG', true). The comment block at lines 22-25 states the detailed handler 'stays on unless an operator explicitly turns it off in the environment file', and line 15 defaults APP_ENV to 'production'.
findings.impact: Laravel's detailed error page renders the environment table, which includes database credentials, APP_KEY, mail and queue secrets, plus source excerpts and the request payload. Any unhandled exception on a production host hands that to the requester, and the comment shows customers are actively asked to capture it.
findings.recommendation: Default to false: (bool) env('APP_DEBUG', false), and set APP_DEBUG=true only in local environment files. Replace the support workflow with a correlation id logged server-side.

triage.reason: The default is the shipped behaviour, and the comment on lines 22-25 states as intent that it is not turned off. This is the opposite of a debug-only path production does not take.
No error handler, middleware or exception renderer in the tree overrides the flag.

findings.title: CORS is configured to accept any origin while carrying credentials
findings.evidence: 'allowed_origins' => ['*'] on line 28 with 'supports_credentials' => true on line 38 and 'allowed_headers' including Authorization. The comment on lines 24-27 states the intent as 'Echoing whatever the browser sends'. Laravel's CORS service reflects the request Origin rather than emitting '*' precisely when credentials are enabled, so this configuration is origin reflection with credentials.
findings.impact: Any web page a portal user visits can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the covered paths and read the responses, turning a drive-by visit into a full read of that customer's billing data and any state-changing endpoint reachable by the listed methods (GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE).
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with the exact origins, resolved from the tenant vanity-domain table at request time and compared in full; never pair a reflected or wildcard origin with supports_credentials.

triage.reason: No origin check exists anywhere else in the tree; the wildcard is the whole policy.
The covered paths carry the session cookie and return invoice data.

Laravel reads CORS settings from config/cors.php and there is no such file here, nor any config('security...') reader in the tree (the only config() call is VerifyWebhookSignature.php:37). Whether a service provider binds this file onto the framework keys cannot be established, so this is capped at probable.

findings.title: Session cookie configured without HttpOnly so page scripts can read it
findings.evidence: 'http_only' => false on line 62, with the comment on lines 58-61 stating the embedded PDF viewer reads the session id out of document.cookie and forwards it on its own XHR. Session encryption is on (line 50) but that protects the payload, not the identifier's exposure to script.
findings.impact: Any script that executes in the page - injected content, a compromised third-party asset, a browser extension - reads the session identifier and replays it, so any XSS in the portal becomes account takeover rather than a bounded defacement.
findings.recommendation: Set http_only to true and give the PDF worker a short-lived, audience-scoped token minted server-side instead of the session cookie.

triage.reason: Nothing else restricts script access to the cookie; the design in the comment depends on script access.
This is not defence in depth behind an equivalent control: HttpOnly is the only mechanism that would keep the identifier out of the DOM.
No config/session.php exists and nothing in the tree reads config('security.session.*'), so whether these keys reach the framework cannot be established here. Capped at probable.

findings.title: Session cookie marked SameSite=None while Secure is disabled
findings.evidence: 'secure' => false on line 68 together with 'same_site' => 'none' on line 70. The comment on lines 65-67 argues the edge load balancer redirects :80 to https, which governs the first request only, not a cookie the browser has already been told it may send in the clear.
findings.impact: The session cookie is transmittable over plain http, so a network position between the client and the edge captures it; and SameSite=None means it rides on every cross-site request, so the cookie is offered on any attacker-initiated navigation. Browsers that enforce the None-requires-Secure rule reject the cookie outright, which also makes this an availability defect.
findings.recommendation: Set secure to true. Keep SameSite=None only if genuine cross-site flows require it, and pair it with Secure; otherwise use Lax.

triage.reason: The 301 at the edge does not retroactively constrain a cookie already issued without the Secure attribute.
Same scope limit as the HttpOnly finding: no config/session.php and no reader for config('security.*') in the tree. Capped at probable.

findings.title: Password reset does not invalidate the account's other sessions
findings.evidence: Lines 93-96 set the new password hash, mark the reset row used and redirect. There is no Auth::logoutOtherDevices, no session-store purge and no remember-token rotation, while the login flow does issue long-lived 'remember' sessions ($request->boolean('remember') at line 31).
findings.impact: A user who resets a password because they believe the account is compromised does not evict the attacker: existing sessions and remember-me cookies stay valid until they expire on their own.
findings.recommendation: After the hash is saved, rotate the remember_token and invalidate the user's server-side sessions.

triage.reason: No listener, observer or middleware in the tree invalidates sessions on a password change.
There is no equivalent control elsewhere; the sessions simply survive.

findings.title: A request header grants administrator rights
findings.evidence: After the JWT is decoded, lines 50-54 read the X-Flags-Elevate request header and line 59 sets is_admin = elevated || claims.roles.contains(admin_claim). The header arrives on the same request as the token and nothing establishes that it came from the internal console: no mTLS check, no shared secret, no trusted-proxy list, no stripping layer in main.rs.
findings.impact: Any caller holding any valid tenant token adds 'X-Flags-Elevate: true' and passes the is_admin gates at routes.rs:112 (upsert) and routes.rs:138 (archive). That grants flag creation, forced 100% rollout, archiving, and control of webhook_url - which is the SSRF sink reported separately.
findings.recommendation: Remove the header path. Derive elevation only from a verified claim, and if on-call impersonation is required, mint a short-lived token for it at the identity provider.

triage.reason: X-Flags-Elevate is an ordinary request header; any HTTP client sets it.
No layer in main.rs strips or validates the header, and no proxy configuration is present in the tree that would.
The boundary crossed is tenant-member to platform administrator, and the same token also carries an arbitrary tenant_id.

findings.title: SQL injection in the flag search term
findings.evidence: The statement is built with format! and line 17 embeds the caller's term directly: "AND (key ILIKE '%{term}%' OR description ILIKE '%{term}%')". term is ListQuery.q (routes.rs:23-24), deserialized straight from the query string with #[serde(default)] and passed through at routes.rs:57. Only tenant_id is bound, as $1 on line 26. The doc comment on lines 4-6 addresses the ORDER BY fragment and says nothing about the term.
findings.impact: A caller closes the literal and rewrites the predicate, which includes the tenant_id = $1 clause that is the isolation boundary. Every tenant's flags, and anything else reachable in the database, become readable.
findings.recommendation: Bind the pattern: keep the ORDER BY fragment from the enums and pass '%' || $2 || '%' as a bound parameter for the ILIKE comparisons.

triage.reason: term is the raw q query parameter; no validation, escaping or allowlist is applied between routes.rs:53 and store.rs:17.
sqlx only parameterises the values passed to .bind(); the format! string is compiled as literal SQL text. The sibling statements at store.rs:37, 58 and 80 show the crate binds when it intends to.

findings.title: Server-side request forgery through the flag's webhook URL
findings.evidence: flag.webhook_url is stored verbatim from the upsert body (model.rs:72, store.rs:74) and posted to at webhook.rs:30 with state.http.post(url). There is no scheme check, no host allowlist, no address-family or private-range filter, and reqwest follows redirects by default. The client is built at main.rs:85 with only a timeout. The trigger is attacker-chosen: upsert with rollout_percent = 100 (routes.rs:124).
findings.impact: An attacker who can reach the upsert route - which, given the X-Flags-Elevate defect, is any token holder - makes the service issue POST requests from inside its own network: cloud metadata endpoints, internal admin panels and databases with HTTP interfaces. routes.rs returns the upstream status via the retry loop's observable timing and the service's own logs, giving a usable oracle for internal scanning.
findings.recommendation: Validate the URL against a fixed allowlist of hosts, require https, resolve the host and reject private, loopback, link-local and metadata addresses after resolution, and disable redirect following on this client.

triage.reason: webhook_url is a free-text field of the request body; config/default.toml:27 states outright that notifications go 'to whatever the flag owner configured'.
No allowlist or egress control exists in the crate, and no network policy is declared in docker-compose.yml.
The outbound call is not a bounded intended exposure: the destination is entirely caller-chosen.

findings.title: Webhook signing falls back to an empty HMAC key
findings.evidence: let secret = std::env::var("FLAGS_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_KEY").unwrap_or_default(); followed by HmacSha256::new_from_slice(secret.as_bytes()).expect("hmac accepts any key size"). The expect message is the point: HMAC accepts a zero-length key, so with the variable unset the function still returns a well-formed hex digest and the caller at line 32 still sets X-Flags-Signature. Nothing anywhere in the crate refuses to start or refuses to send when the key is absent.
findings.impact: A receiver that verifies X-Flags-Signature is verifying an HMAC under a key anyone can guess, so any party can forge a rollout notification for any tenant. The control runs on every call and cannot fail, which is why a reviewer reads the header as proof the channel is authenticated.
findings.recommendation: Load the key once at start-up and fail to boot when it is missing or shorter than 32 bytes; skip signing rather than emitting a header signed with an empty key.

triage.reason: The empty key is not a placeholder that breaks loudly - unwrap_or_default() makes it the silent success path.
No start-up validation of FLAGS_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_KEY exists in main.rs, and docker-compose.yml does not set the variable for the api service.
There is no second integrity control on the notification; this signature is the only one.

findings.title: The API container mounts the host Docker socket
findings.evidence: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock on the api service, justified by the comment on lines 16-17 that a rollout job shells out to docker restart. No code in edge-flags/src uses std::process, Command or any container API; a search for those symbols across the crate returns nothing.
findings.impact: Write access to the Docker socket is root on the host: any code execution inside the api container - reachable via the SQL injection and the SSRF in the same service - escalates to full host compromise, including the database volume and every other container.
findings.recommendation: Remove the mount. If restarting workers is genuinely required, put it behind a narrow, authenticated sidecar that exposes only that one operation, or use a scoped orchestrator API.

triage.reason: The stated justification is not substantiated in the tree: no process invocation exists anywhere in edge-flags/src, so the container is not a documented system container performing that function.
The boundary crossed is container to host, and the api container terminates untrusted HTTP requests.
No socket proxy, seccomp profile or user namespace remapping is declared in the compose file.

findings.title: Database password hardcoded in the compose file, bypassing the secret it defines
findings.evidence: FLAGS__DATABASE__URL: postgres://flags:flags-svc-2024@db:5432/flags on line 11 and again on line 46 for the migrate service. The same file defines a docker secret for exactly this value (lines 31-33 and 52-54): the db service reads POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE from /run/secrets/flags_db_password while the two consumers carry the literal.
findings.impact: The database password is in version control and in the environment of two containers, readable through docker inspect and any process listing of the container environment. The secret mechanism the file sets up gives no protection because the clients do not use it.
findings.recommendation: Read the password from the mounted secret in both consumers (or from an env_file kept out of version control), and rotate the value, which is compromised from the moment it was committed.

triage.reason: 'flags-svc-2024' is a concrete credential, not a ${VAR} placeholder, and it must match the secret file for the stack to start.
The file is a deployment artifact: it pins an internal registry image at 0.6.2 with restart: unless-stopped, not a throwaway dev harness.

findings.title: The JWT decoding key is built from the issuer URL, so token verification cannot work as written
findings.evidence: DecodingKey::from_rsa_pem(state.settings.auth.issuer.as_bytes()). auth.issuer is a URL - config/default.toml:16 sets it to https://id.internal.example/realms/platform - and the AuthCfg struct (main.rs:31-36) declares no key or JWKS field at all. The comment on lines 32-33 describes a cached PEM that the configuration does not carry.
findings.impact: Parsing a URL as an RSA PEM fails, so every authenticated route answers 500 'signing key unavailable' rather than validating anything. The direction of failure is closed, so this is not an exploitable bypass today - but the service's entire authentication path has never been exercised, and the natural fix of pointing from_rsa_pem at whatever string is available is where a real bypass lands.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit auth.public_key (or a JWKS URL with caching) to AuthCfg, build the DecodingKey once at start-up, and fail to boot if it does not parse rather than failing per request.

triage.reason: There is no reading under which a realm URL is a PEM: the same value is simultaneously passed to validation.set_issuer at auth.rs:41, so one string cannot be both.
This is the only code path to the decoding key; there is no alternative branch.
The finding is not downgraded to a non-issue by an equivalent control - it is reported at low precisely because the failure is closed.

findings.title: Database and token-validation error strings are returned to the caller
findings.evidence: Five handlers map internal errors into the response body with e.to_string(): lines 59, 73, 78, 93, 100, 122, 144 and 149. Authentication failures do the same at line 46, returning the jsonwebtoken crate's own rejection message. sqlx error strings carry the PostgreSQL server message, which names relations, columns and constraint identifiers, and for a failed cast can echo the offending value.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated or low-privileged caller maps the schema and the token-validation logic from error text, which lowers the cost of the injection already present in store.rs and of token forgery attempts.
findings.recommendation: Return a fixed message with a correlation id and log the detail server-side; keep the jsonwebtoken reason out of the 401 body.

triage.reason: Schema identifiers and validation internals are reconnaissance material, not public content.
No error-shaping layer sits in front: main.rs adds only TraceLayer and CORS, so these strings are what the client receives.

findings.title: JWT signature validation is replaced by a validator that accepts every token
findings.evidence: SignatureValidator = (token, _) => new JwtSecurityToken(token). A custom SignatureValidator replaces signature checking entirely in Microsoft.IdentityModel: whatever it returns is treated as the validated token, so the IssuerSigningKey configured on line 28 is never consulted. The delegate simply re-parses the string. The comment on lines 32-34 gives cold-start latency as the reason. These parameters are what Program.cs:24 installs on the only authentication scheme the app registers.
findings.impact: Anyone can mint a token: base64 a header and a payload with iss and aud copied from appsettings.json (both are non-secret), add role=fleet-admin and any tenant_id, and append arbitrary bytes as the signature. That yields full administrative access across every tenant - device listing and registration, firmware promotion to any channel including Factory - with no credential at all.
findings.recommendation: Delete the SignatureValidator override. Configure the JWKS metadata address so the middleware caches the rotating keys itself (that is what the cold-start comment is actually asking for), and keep ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true.

triage.reason: This is the control: the fallback authorization policy at Program.cs:31-33 requires an authenticated user, and this delegate is what decides who is authenticated.
BuildValidationParameters is called unconditionally at Program.cs:24 with no environment guard; there is no second code path.

It is not a hook the framework wraps with a real check - SignatureValidator is documented as the replacement for signature validation, and the surrounding ValidateIssuer/ValidateAudience settings are what makes it read as complete.

findings.title: Production disables token expiry and sets a 24-hour clock skew
findings.evidence: "ValidateLifetime": false and "ClockSkewMinutes": 1440 in the production settings file, read at TokenService.cs:29-30 into TokenValidationParameters. The base appsettings.json sets the opposite (true / 2). The _note on line 14 gives buffered gateway telemetry as the reason.
findings.impact: Tokens never expire, so a token captured from a gateway, a log or a support bundle grants access permanently. There is no revocation list, no jti check against a store and no reference-token introspection anywhere in the service, so a leaked credential cannot be withdrawn at all.
findings.recommendation: Keep ValidateLifetime = true with a small skew, and handle backhaul buffering by validating the telemetry timestamp inside the payload rather than by suspending token expiry for the whole API.

triage.reason: The setting is in appsettings.Production.json, which FleetApi.csproj:24-26 copies to the output directory; this is the shipped configuration.
No revocation store, jti replay cache or introspection endpoint exists in the tree to compensate.
There is no server-side session that bounds the token's life independently.

findings.title: Production SQL Server credentials committed in appsettings.Production.json
findings.evidence: "Server=sql-fleet-prod.internal,1433;Database=Fleet;User Id=fleet_app;Password=Fl33tSvc-2024-prod;...". The password is a literal, the host name is a production host, and FleetApi.csproj:24-26 marks this file CopyToOutputDirectory so it also ships inside the build artifact. The project declares a UserSecretsId (csproj:8) and appsettings.json:17 states that the JWT key comes from user secrets and the environment - the same mechanism was available for this value and was not used.
findings.impact: Anyone with repository read access, or with the published build output, holds the production database account. The value is compromised from the moment it was committed and cannot be un-published by editing the file.
findings.recommendation: Move the connection string to the environment or a secret store, rotate fleet_app's password, and audit database access since the commit that introduced it.

triage.reason: It is a concrete password against a named production host, not a placeholder.
The filename declares the environment and the csproj copies it into what ships.
It grants access to the fleet database.

findings.title: SQL injection in the device serial search via FromSqlRaw
findings.evidence: FromSqlRaw($"SELECT TOP 25 * FROM devices WHERE tenant_id = {TenantId} AND serial LIKE '%{q}%' ORDER BY serial"). Because the argument is a plain string, the C# interpolation is performed before EF Core sees it, so q is baked into the SQL text - FromSqlRaw does not parameterise. The parameterising overloads (FromSql / FromSqlInterpolated) are the ones that would have. q is [FromQuery] string with only a null-or-whitespace check on line 47.
findings.impact: The caller rewrites the predicate, including the tenant_id filter, and on SQL Server can append stacked statements after the terminator. Every tenant's device inventory is readable and the connection's account can write.
findings.recommendation: Use FromSqlInterpolated with the same interpolated string (which produces bound parameters), or FromSqlRaw with explicit SqlParameter arguments for both tenant_id and the LIKE pattern.

triage.reason: q comes from the query string and reaches line 54 unfiltered.
No layer parameterises here: the sibling actions on lines 30 and 67 use LINQ, which does parameterise, which is exactly why this one stands out.
FromSqlRaw is documented as executing the string as given; the parameterising behaviour belongs to the FormattableString overload that is not used here.

findings.title: Device retirement is unauthenticated and reaches every tenant's devices
findings.evidence: [AllowAnonymous] on the DELETE /api/devices/{id} action, which overrides the FallbackPolicy registered at Program.cs:31-33 (the fallback applies only where no authorization metadata is present). Inside, line 102 is FirstOrDefaultAsync(d => d.Id == id) with no TenantId predicate, unlike every sibling in the file - List (line 31), Search (line 54) and Stats (line 68) all filter on TenantId. The comment on lines 93-97 justifies the anonymity by an incomplete SSO hop.
findings.impact: Any caller on the internet retires any device in the fleet by walking the id space: a single unauthenticated request removes a device from every listing, and a loop takes the whole fleet offline from the console's point of view. There is no authentication to attribute the action to and no tenant boundary to contain it.
findings.recommendation: Remove [AllowAnonymous], scope the lookup to the caller's TenantId the way the siblings do, and fix the console flow so it calls this after the SSO hop completes.

triage.reason: The fallback policy is the mandatory layer and [AllowAnonymous] is precisely the opt-out from it; nothing else in the pipeline (Program.cs:57-70) re-imposes it.
The route is served on the same public listener as the rest of the controller, and it is state-changing, not a probe.
Two boundaries are crossed at once: unauthenticated to authenticated, and tenant to tenant.

findings.title: Production MQTT broker configured without TLS
findings.evidence: "BrokerUri": "tcp://mqtt-fleet-prod.internal:1883" with "TlsRequired": false and a "Username": "fleet-api", against the base appsettings.json which uses tls://...:8883 with TlsRequired true. The _note on line 19 gives VPC co-location and un-reflashed gateways as the reason. MQTTnet.AspNetCore is referenced at FleetApi.csproj:18.
findings.impact: Fleet telemetry and the broker credentials travel unencrypted and unauthenticated on the internal network, so anyone with a network position there reads device data and can publish commands as the API. 'Same subnet' is not a confidentiality control.
findings.recommendation: Restore tls:// on 8883 with certificate validation; where gateways cannot yet carry the CA bundle, terminate them on a separate listener and bridge it rather than downgrading the API's own connection.

triage.reason: Same-subnet placement bounds who can reach it but not who can read it; no network policy artifact is present that would.
No code in the tree reads the Mqtt section, so whether these keys are consumed by the shipped host cannot be established here. Per the cap this is reported as probable rather than confirmed.

findings.title: Unvalidated device serial written into a line-oriented log
findings.evidence: _log.LogInformation("Device {Serial} retired", device.Serial). Serial reaches the row from the DeviceRegistration body at line 82 with no validation of length or character set (the record on line 117 declares it as a bare string), so it can carry CR/LF. The write is triggered by the [AllowAnonymous] action, so no credential is needed to fire it. Serilog is configured from configuration only (Program.cs:11) and neither appsettings file declares a sink or a formatter.
findings.impact: One request forges additional log records: an attacker registers a device whose serial embeds a newline and a plausible line, then triggers the retire path, and the fabricated record appears in the aggregator. Where the log is rendered in a viewer, the same value reaches the page as markup.
findings.recommendation: Constrain Serial at registration to the real serial alphabet, and configure Serilog with a structured sink whose consumer parses that format rather than splitting on newlines.

triage.reason: Serial is caller-supplied at registration with no pattern, length bound or allowlist between the body and the column.

Neither appsettings.json nor appsettings.Production.json declares a Serilog sink or output template, so whether the emitted format escapes control characters, and whether its consumer parses that format, cannot be established from the tree. Per the cap this is reported as probable.
Even where the sink cannot re-execute the value, the accountability loss stands: the record cannot be attributed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated-input pickle deserialization from a client cookie
findings.evidence: saved = pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(raw_cookie)) where raw_cookie is request.COOKIES.get('hd_filters') read on line 48. The cookie is an ordinary cookie, not a signed one - Django signs only get_signed_cookie/set_signed_cookie - and there is no HMAC, no allowlist and no format check. The try/except on lines 51-54 catches the exception after unpickling, which is after the payload has already run: pickle executes __reduce__ during load.
findings.impact: Remote code execution on the web tier as the application user. Any user who can sign in (or anyone who can set a cookie in a victim's browser for this host, since the value is attacker-chosen and never validated) runs arbitrary Python inside the Django process, which holds the database credentials and the export volume.
findings.recommendation: Store the layout as JSON and parse it with json.loads under a schema, or move it to the server-side session. If a client-held blob is required, sign it and verify the signature before parsing.

triage.reason: The value is a request cookie; nothing between line 48 and line 52 constrains it.
pickle reconstructs arbitrary objects and executes during reconstruction; this is the sink class itself, not a parser.
No integrity verification precedes the call. Django's SECRET_KEY-based signing is available and not used here, and the settings do not enable any cookie-signing middleware.

findings.title: Command injection through the export filename
findings.evidence: subprocess.run(f"zip -j -q {dest} {tmp_path}", shell=True, check=True) where dest = os.path.join(settings.EXPORT_ROOT, filename + '.zip') on line 40. filename arrives from views.py:96 as request.GET.get('filename', ...) and is handed to the task at views.py:98 with no validation, no shlex.quote and no character allowlist. Contrast the sibling task at tasks.py:59, whose argument is a uuid plus an allowlisted extension - the project knows the difference and applied it in one place only.
findings.impact: Shell metacharacters in the query string execute as the Celery worker. And the trigger is a GET (urls.py:16) protected only by a Lax SameSite cookie (settings.py:114), so a cross-site image or link fires the job as any signed-in agent, turning this into drive-by code execution on the worker host. Path traversal is available on the same parameter: an absolute filename replaces EXPORT_ROOT entirely in os.path.join.
findings.recommendation: Drop shell=True and pass an argument list: subprocess.run(['zip','-j','-q',dest,tmp_path], check=True). Independently, derive the stored name server-side and keep the agent's chosen name for the Content-Disposition header only; make the export a POST.

triage.reason: filename is a raw query parameter at views.py:96 and reaches the f-string unmodified.
No sanitiser sits between the view and the task; the Celery boundary serialises the string verbatim.
This is a real shell string - shell=True is explicit on line 42 - not a list form that only resembles one.

findings.title: Django DEBUG defaults to on in the production settings module
findings.evidence: DEBUG = os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG", "1") == "1" - the default is the enabled state. That this is the production module is established in the same file: ALLOWED_HOSTS defaults to helpdesk.northgate.example (line 27) and CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS is the https production origin (line 30). The comment on lines 17-18 states that agents paste the error page into escalation tickets.
findings.impact: Django's debug page renders the full settings dictionary, the SQL query history and local variables for every frame. That discloses SECRET_KEY, the database password from the PG* environment, the Celery broker URL and ticket contents to whoever triggers an exception - and the workflow in the comment moves that page into ticket bodies.
findings.recommendation: Default to off: os.environ.get("DJANGO_DEBUG", "0") == "1". Give agents a correlation id in the 500 page and keep the trace in the server log or in Sentry, which is already a dependency (requirements.txt:11).

triage.reason: The default is what ships when the variable is absent, and no separate production settings module exists in the tree to override it.
No middleware or handler in the MIDDLEWARE list (settings.py:42-54) suppresses the debug response.

findings.title: A usable SECRET_KEY is committed as the settings fallback
findings.evidence: SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get("DJANGO_SECRET_KEY", "django-insecure-hd-6f2b1c9a4d7e0b5318ca77e2049fbd6c"). Django does not reject the fallback; it is used silently when the variable is unset. The same module points at the production host (line 27) and uses the cache-backed session engine (line 111), whose contents are signed with this key.
findings.impact: Where the environment variable is absent, session cookies, CSRF tokens, password-reset tokens and every signed value in the application are forgeable from a value published in the repository - which is authentication bypass for any account. Regardless of deployment, the key is compromised because it was versioned.
findings.recommendation: Remove the default so start-up fails without DJANGO_SECRET_KEY, and rotate the key (which invalidates existing sessions and reset links, as intended).

triage.reason: It is a complete, usable key, not a ${VAR} placeholder; the django-insecure- prefix is a naming convention, not an enforcement.
No .env, compose file, systemd unit or CI configuration is in the tree, so whether the deployed environment sets DJANGO_SECRET_KEY cannot be established. Per the cap this is reported as probable.

findings.title: Session and CSRF cookies configured to travel over plain HTTP
findings.evidence: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = False and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = False, with the comment on lines 116-117 stating that TLS stops at the branch-office proxy and the last hop is plain http. Enumerating the rest of the security block key by key: SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS and SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER are all absent, so SecurityMiddleware (line 43) enforces nothing beyond the nosniff header set on line 121.
findings.impact: Session and CSRF cookies are transmitted in the clear on the internal hop and on any http request the browser makes to this host, so a network position anywhere between the proxy and the app servers yields session hijacking. The absence of HSTS means a downgrade is not prevented at the browser either.
findings.recommendation: Terminate TLS at the app servers or run the last hop over TLS, then set both flags to True, add SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER for the proxy, and enable SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT with SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS.

triage.reason: The comment identifies the plaintext hop rather than a compensating control, and no other setting in the module restores confidentiality.
Anyone on the path between the proxy and the app servers is a second principal.

findings.title: Open redirect on the sign-in next parameter
findings.evidence: return redirect(request.GET.get("next", settings.LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL)) with no call to django.utils.http.url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme and no host comparison. The middleware only ever writes request.path into next (middleware.py:18), but the attacker constructs the sign-in URL directly, so the parameter's real domain is arbitrary.
findings.impact: A link to https://helpdesk.northgate.example/accounts/login/?next=https://attacker.example carries the help desk's own hostname through the credential prompt and lands the agent on the attacker's page immediately after a successful sign-in - a high-credibility phishing and token-relay primitive against exactly the staff who administer tickets.
findings.recommendation: Validate before redirecting: if not url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme(nxt, allowed_hosts={request.get_host()}, require_https=request.is_secure()): nxt = settings.LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL.

triage.reason: django.shortcuts.redirect performs no host validation; HttpResponseRedirect.allowed_schemes blocks javascript: but permits any http(s) host.
next is read directly from request.GET on line 33; the middleware is not the only writer because the URL is reachable directly.

findings.title: Admin delete permission granted unconditionally to any staff user
findings.evidence: def has_delete_permission(self, request, obj=None): return True on the base class inherited by QueueAdmin, TicketAdmin, CommentAdmin and AttachmentAdmin. ModelAdmin.has_delete_permission is the check Django consults; returning True unconditionally replaces the per-model delete permission for the object view and for the bulk 'delete selected' action. The asymmetry is inside the same file: OrganizationAdmin overrides it correctly on line 33 with request.user.is_superuser, so the pattern was known and applied once.
findings.impact: Any user flagged is_staff can delete tickets, comments, attachments and queues within their organisation regardless of the Django permissions assigned to them, individually or in bulk, and Ticket deletion cascades to comments and attachments (models.py:59, 67). The get_queryset scoping bounds which rows are reachable; it does not decide who may delete them.
findings.recommendation: Delete the override and let Django's model permissions apply, or gate it on a real predicate such as request.user.has_perm(f'tickets.delete_{self.model._meta.model_name}').

triage.reason: get_queryset (line 16) scopes the row set, not the verb; there is no second permission layer between the admin view and the delete.
The boundary is between staff roles inside one organisation - a support agent and a support lead are different principals with different permission sets.
There is no equivalent server-side permission check elsewhere; this override is the decision point.

findings.title: No rate limiting or lockout on the sign-in handler
findings.evidence: login_view calls authenticate() on every POST with no attempt counter, no backoff and no lockout. The MIDDLEWARE list (settings.py:42-54) contains no throttling component, requirements.txt declares no rate-limiting package such as django-axes or django-ratelimit, and a search of the tree for ratelimit, throttle, axes and lockout returns nothing. Compare billing-portal, where the login route carries throttle:5,1 (routes/web.php:22).
findings.impact: Unlimited credential-stuffing and brute-force attempts against staff accounts, at whatever rate the worker pool sustains, with no signal to defenders - the failure path does not even log the attempt.
findings.recommendation: Add per-identity and per-IP throttling with progressive backoff (django-axes or a cache-backed counter keyed on the username), and log failed attempts.

triage.reason: No throttling exists in the middleware stack, in the view, or as a dependency; the enumeration above is exhaustive for this tree.
An edge WAF or proxy could rate-limit /accounts/login/, but no such artifact is present, and per the rule the absence of evidence is not HOLDS. The finding is reported at medium on the code as given.

findings.title: SECURITY DEFINER function without a fixed search_path writes to unqualified tables
findings.evidence: post_journal is declared LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER (lines 34-35) with no SET search_path clause, and its three writes name their tables unqualified: INSERT INTO journals (line 56), INSERT INTO entries (line 60), INSERT INTO audit_log (line 68). The function is owned by ledger_owner (line 111) and EXECUTE is granted to ledger_app (004_grants.sql:27). Both of its neighbours do the opposite: archive_account carries SET search_path = ledger, pg_temp (line 84) and fully qualifies every object, and current_tenant() carries SET search_path = pg_catalog, pg_temp (002_rls.sql:24).
findings.impact: The caller controls name resolution inside a function running as the schema owner. ledger_app sets its own search_path, or creates a temporary table named journals, entries or audit_log - pg_temp is searched ahead of the rest of the path when the path is not pinned - and the definer's writes land on objects the caller defines. That is arbitrary action with ledger_owner's privileges, which is the role the RLS design places above the tenant policies.
findings.recommendation: Add SET search_path = ledger, pg_temp to the function and schema-qualify all three INSERT targets, matching archive_account exactly.

triage.reason: No control constrains the caller's search_path: the pooler's server_reset_query does not run in transaction mode (pgbouncer.ini:18-19), and RLS does not govern name resolution.
The reading is settled by the two siblings in the same file that do pin the path and do qualify their objects; the omission here is a difference, not a convention.
search_path is session state the ledger_app role sets for itself, and EXECUTE on this function is granted to that role.

findings.title: Tenant isolation depends on a session variable behind a transaction-pooling pooler
findings.evidence: pool_mode = transaction with server_reset_query = DISCARD ALL. pgbouncer runs server_reset_query only in session pooling unless server_reset_query_always is set, and it is not set here - so the reset does not run. Meanwhile every RLS policy in 002_rls.sql resolves through ledger.current_tenant(), which reads current_setting('app.tenant_id') (line 26), and the file header on lines 3-5 states that the value is applied 'right after checkout (see the pool's on-connect hook)'. An on-connect hook has connection lifetime; under transaction pooling a backend is reassigned between transactions.
findings.impact: A backend that carries app.tenant_id from one client's transaction is handed to the next client's transaction still holding that value. Because the setting is the sole input to every policy, the next tenant reads and writes the previous tenant's accounts, journals, entries and audit rows. The failure is silent and intermittent, and it defeats the entire RLS design rather than one policy.
findings.recommendation: Set the GUC with SET LOCAL inside each transaction rather than on connect, and make it mandatory: have the application fail closed when app.tenant_id is unset. If the on-connect model must stay, switch to session pooling or set server_reset_query_always = 1.

triage.reason: DISCARD ALL is configured but inert in this pool mode, which is the WEB-27 shape: a control that is present, is read as proof, and never runs.

The application's connection code is not in this tree, so whether it issues SET or SET LOCAL cannot be established here - the comment says 'on checkout', which is the failing shape, but the code would settle it. Per the cap this is reported as probable.
The boundary is tenant to tenant, which is the boundary the whole 002_rls.sql file exists to enforce.

findings.title: Provisioning fetches migrations over plain HTTP and executes them unverified
findings.evidence: MIGRATION_MIRROR is http:// (line 17). Line 48 curls ${MIGRATION_MIRROR}/${ENVIRONMENT}/latest.tar.gz, line 49 extracts it, and lines 82-86 run every *.sql it contained through psql -U ledger_owner against the production database. There is no TLS, no checksum, no signature and no manifest of expected files anywhere in the script.
findings.impact: Anyone able to answer or intercept that HTTP request - a DNS answer, an ARP position, a proxy, a stale internal name - executes arbitrary SQL as the schema owner on the ledger database: create a role, disable a policy, exfiltrate or alter financial records. The path runs on every provisioning run and needs no credential.
findings.recommendation: Fetch over https, verify a detached signature or a pinned SHA-256 against a manifest before extraction, and refuse to apply anything that fails verification.

triage.reason: The archive contents are the input, and they arrive from the network with no integrity check; only the URL prefix is a constant.
No verification step exists between line 48 and line 85; ON_ERROR_STOP is an error-handling flag, not an authenticity check.
An internal mirror bounds who can normally reach it but does not authenticate what comes back, and the script places no network control around the fetch.

findings.title: Downloaded archive extracted without validating entry paths
findings.evidence: tar -xzf "${STAGE_DIR}/extra.tar.gz" -C "${STAGE_DIR}" with no --no-same-owner, no --no-same-permissions and no prior listing or path check. GNU tar strips a leading / but does not by itself prevent ../ traversal in member names, and the script runs with enough privilege to write /etc/ledger, /etc/pgbouncer and /srv (lines 38, 99, 118).
findings.impact: A crafted archive from the unauthenticated mirror writes outside the staging directory - a systemd unit, a cron entry, an authorized_keys file, or the pgbouncer configuration the script installs moments later - which converts the same fetch into persistent host compromise rather than one-off SQL execution.
findings.recommendation: List and validate member paths before extracting (reject any containing .. or an absolute prefix), extract with --no-same-owner --no-same-permissions into a scratch directory, then copy only the expected *.sql files across.

triage.reason: The archive is fetched from a plain-HTTP mirror on line 48, so its member names are attacker-influenceable.
No path validation, chroot or unprivileged extraction user is applied; -C only sets the working directory.

findings.title: Database credentials written to a world-readable file
findings.evidence: Lines 59-65 write /etc/ledger/db.env containing LEDGER_DB_PASSWORD from the secret store, and line 69 sets mode 0644 on it. The comment on lines 67-68 gives the reason: three consumers that do not share a group. The file is consumed by backup.sh:14, which sources it and uses the password on line 22.
findings.impact: Every local account on the host reads the ledger application's database password, including any service account a web or batch process runs under. It defeats the point of fetching the value from Vault two lines earlier, and it turns any low-privileged local foothold into full database access.
findings.recommendation: Set mode 0640 with a dedicated group and add each consumer to that group, or hand the value to each consumer through its own unit's EnvironmentFile / systemd credential rather than through one shared file.

triage.reason: Every unprivileged local account is a second principal, and the comment states there are three distinct service identities on the host.
The intended sharing is with three named consumers; 0644 grants it to all of them plus everyone else, which is not the bounded exposure.
It is a live production database password.

findings.title: Export directory made world-writable
findings.evidence: chmod -R 0777 "$EXPORT_DIR" on /srv/ledger/exports. The comment on lines 111-115 explains that the API, the reporting sidecar, the nightly archiver and the ops jobs all use the directory under different accounts.
findings.impact: Statement bundles - ledger data, which is financial and identifying - are readable by every local account, and writable too: any local process can alter a statement before the archiver picks it up, or drop a file the downstream jobs consume. The recursive form also relaxes anything already in the directory.
findings.recommendation: Create a shared group for the four consumers, set the directory to 2770 with the setgid bit so new files inherit the group, and set files to 0660.

triage.reason: Every local account on the host is a second principal; the four named consumers are only some of them.
The intent is sharing among four service accounts, and 0777 is not a bounded form of that.
The bundles carry ledger records, which is exactly the data the RLS policies elsewhere in this project exist to compartmentalise.

findings.title: Role passwords passed on the psql command line
findings.evidence: psql ... -c "ALTER ROLE ledger_app PASSWORD '${APP_PASSWORD}'" -c "ALTER ROLE ledger_report PASSWORD '${REPORT_PASSWORD}'". The values are interpolated into argv, so they appear in the process table for the life of the command; and ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD in plaintext is recorded verbatim by the server whenever log_statement is set to ddl or all. The single-quoting is also unescaped, so a password containing an apostrophe breaks the statement or extends it.
findings.impact: Any local user running ps during provisioning captures both role passwords, and any operator with read access to the PostgreSQL logs recovers them afterwards from a file nobody thinks of as a secret store.
findings.recommendation: Pipe the statements into psql on stdin instead of using -c, use \password or a properly quoted parameter, and confirm log_statement is not set to ddl or all on the target while provisioning runs.

triage.reason: Any other local account can read /proc and the process table; the PostgreSQL log has its own separate readership.
The values are real credentials fetched from Vault at lines 55-56, not placeholders.
Nothing in the script suppresses the argv exposure - PGPASSWORD is correctly kept in the environment at line 75, which shows the safe idiom was available and not applied here.

findings.title: The application role holds direct INSERT on the audit log the definer functions exist to protect

location.symbol: GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES TO ledger_app

findings.evidence: GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA ledger TO ledger_app, plus the same defaults at lines 14-15. That includes ledger.audit_log, and the audit_append policy (002_rls.sql:83-85) permits any INSERT whose tenant_id matches the session. The comment at 003_functions.sql:25-26 states the opposite intent: post_journal runs SECURITY DEFINER 'so the API role does not need direct insert rights on ledger.audit_log'.
findings.impact: The application role writes audit records directly, so the audit trail carries no more authority than the application it is meant to hold to account: a compromised or buggy API forges journal.posted and account.archived entries, or pads the log to bury a real one. The stated design guarantee does not hold. UPDATE and DELETE on the same table are blocked, but by RLS having no policy for those commands rather than by the grant.
findings.recommendation: Grant table privileges explicitly per table rather than with ON ALL TABLES, and give ledger_app only SELECT on audit_log, leaving INSERT to the definer functions as the comment describes.

triage.reason: The RLS policy permits the insert rather than preventing it; there is no other layer between ledger_app and the table.
The exposure is not the intended one - the intent is recorded in the code and is the opposite.
There is no second, independent audit sink that would make this defence in depth.

findings.title: The session cookie is unsigned base64 JSON and is trusted for identity, workspace and role
findings.evidence: readSession base64url-decodes the cookie, JSON.parses it, and returns userId, workspaceId and role straight from the parsed object (lines 27-44). writeSession (line 51) is the exact inverse with no signing step. There is no HMAC, no encryption and no key: package.json declares no jose, iron-session, next-auth or cookie-signing dependency, and no createHmac call exists in lib/. The only integrity-shaped check is the issuedAt window on line 34, and issuedAt comes from the same forgeable blob. All three consumers - middleware.ts:27, app/actions/notes.ts:22 and app/api/share/route.ts:36 - use the result directly.
findings.impact: Anyone constructs a cookie: base64url of {"userId":"...","workspaceId":"<any>","role":"admin","issuedAt":<now>} and is authenticated as any user, in any workspace, at any role. The middleware admits them, the server actions read and write that workspace's notes, and every other authorization decision in the app rests on these fields. This is complete authentication bypass with no credential.
findings.recommendation: Replace the format with a signed or encrypted cookie - a JWT verified with a server key, or an encrypted session such as iron-session - and verify it before any field is read; or move to opaque session ids resolved against a server-side store.

triage.reason: No verification layer exists: middleware.ts calls readSession itself and there is no signing utility anywhere in the tree.
Next.js cookies() returns the raw cookie value; it performs no signing or verification of its own.
The cookie is entirely client-supplied - that is the definition of the sink here.

findings.title: The middleware reflects any request Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
findings.evidence: Lines 13-19 read the Origin header and set Access-Control-Allow-Origin to that exact value together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, for every request the matcher covers. There is no allowlist, no suffix check and no comparison of any kind; the comment on lines 10-12 states reflection as the intent. The matcher (line 45) covers every page route.
findings.impact: Any page a signed-in user visits reads authenticated responses from this workspace cross-origin, because the browser attaches the session cookie and the reflected header authorises the read. Combined with the note pages returning any note by id, that is a full read of the workspace's content from a drive-by visit.
findings.recommendation: Compare the Origin against a fixed allowlist of the desktop, extension and marketing origins, echo it only on a match, and set Vary: Origin (which is already done) so caches do not mix responses.

triage.reason: The reflection is unconditional; next.config.mjs's serverActions.allowedOrigins (line 9) constrains server actions only, not page GETs or route handlers.
The covered responses are the user's own notes, rendered with the session cookie attached.

findings.title: The share route handler is unauthenticated and performs no ownership check
findings.evidence: The handler fetches the note at line 30 with getNote(body.noteId) - a lookup by id alone (lib/db.ts:20) with no workspace or owner predicate - and then posts its title and rendered html to the target. The session is read at line 36, after the note has already been loaded, and is never branched on: it feeds only recordShare's audit column with a session?.userId ?? 'unknown' fallback (line 49). Nothing authenticates the caller, because middleware.ts:45 excludes api from its matcher, so no route handler in this app sees the middleware at all.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller who holds any note id pushes that note's contents to one of the configured integrations and writes a forged share record attributed to 'unknown'. The id is the only barrier, and it is not an access control: the note page discloses ids to any signed-in user across workspaces, and the reflected-CORS defect exposes them cross-origin. The session read on line 36 is what makes the handler read as authenticated in review.
findings.recommendation: Require a session before anything else and return 401 when it is absent, then load the note scoped to that session's workspaceId and reject when it does not match.

triage.reason: The middleware that would have supplied the gate explicitly excludes api at middleware.ts:45; there is no other guard in the request path.

noteId is a body field. The target is allowlisted by isAllowedShareTarget (lib/policy.ts:13) - which is why this is reported as an authorization defect and not as SSRF - but the note being read is entirely caller-chosen.
Two boundaries are crossed: unauthenticated to authenticated, and workspace to workspace.

findings.title: Any signed-in user can read any workspace's note by id
findings.evidence: getNote(params.id) with no session or workspace comparison, in both the page (line 16) and generateMetadata (line 10). lib/db.ts:20 resolves the row by id alone. The sibling query in the same module, listNotes (lib/db.ts:29-37), does filter WHERE workspace_id = $1, and the server action that calls it passes session.workspaceId (app/actions/notes.ts:35) - so the scoping exists in the codebase and is simply not applied on this path. The middleware admits any session-bearing request to /notes/*.
findings.impact: Any user with a session - and, given the unsigned cookie, that is anyone - reads any note in any workspace, including its title through the page metadata. That is a complete cross-tenant read of the product's core content.
findings.recommendation: Read the session in the page, load the note scoped to its workspaceId, and call notFound() when it does not match.

triage.reason: The middleware checks that a session exists, not whose note this is; no query-level tenant filter is applied by lib/db.ts on this path, and listNotes in the same file shows the scope is applied deliberately elsewhere.
/notes/[id] is behind the session wall, not one of the PUBLIC_PREFIXES (middleware.ts:5); it is not a public-by-design surface.
Notes are the users' private content.

findings.title: Note updates authenticate the caller but never check the note is theirs
findings.evidence: Line 58 is currentSession(); on a line of its own - the return value is discarded, so the call only asserts that some session exists. The note is then fetched by id (line 66) and written (line 72) with no comparison against the session's workspaceId or userId. The two sibling actions in the same file do bind it: createNoteAction passes session.workspaceId and session.userId (line 46), recentNotes passes session.workspaceId (line 35). saveNote (lib/db.ts:46-52) has no workspace predicate of its own.
findings.impact: Any user with a session overwrites the title and body of any note in any workspace, with no trace beyond updated_at. That is cross-tenant data destruction and content forgery, and the discarded currentSession() call is what makes the handler read as authorized.
findings.recommendation: Keep the session: const session = currentSession(); then load the note scoped to session.workspaceId and reject when it does not match, or push the predicate into saveNote so it cannot be forgotten.

triage.reason: currentSession() proves only that a session exists; no ORM-level or database-level scope applies, as saveNote's SQL at lib/db.ts:47-50 shows.
input.id is a form field validated only as a uuid (line 12).
There is no equivalent server-side ownership check anywhere on this path.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy on an app that renders stored HTML
findings.evidence: The headers() block sets X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy and X-Frame-Options for /:path* and no Content-Security-Policy. The app injects stored markup into the page with dangerouslySetInnerHTML (app/notes/[id]/page.tsx:33). The renderer is correctly configured (markdown-it with html:false plus a link-scheme allowlist at lib/policy.ts:34-64), so this is defence in depth rather than a live injection.
findings.impact: Nothing constrains script execution if the renderer's configuration is later relaxed, if a markdown-it parsing gap is found, or if any other injection path reaches the page - and it is the layer that would also bound the damage of the unsigned-session and reflected-CORS defects in this same app.
findings.recommendation: Add a Content-Security-Policy with a nonce-based script-src, object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none', alongside the three headers already configured.

triage.reason: The rule would downgrade this to informational if the missing control were not load-bearing; it is reported at low, not dismissed, precisely because the render path uses dangerouslySetInnerHTML.
No CSP is emitted anywhere else - there is no middleware header, no meta tag and no other headers() entry in the config.
